title: A son's rites for Jatayu
hookLine: a prince gives a dying bird the rites of a son
carry: the last rites honor love, not only blood
last: LIFE MAY GO, THE WORD MUST NOT.

cards: Rama comes back from killing the deer, meets Lakshmana on the path, and knows before he gets there. The hut is empty. Valmiki lets Rama come apart.
He runs from tree to tree asking where she went. He asks the river. He asks the deer, and the deer turn and look south.
His grief turns to rage, and he says he'll tear the worlds apart, until Lakshmana talks him down. Then, on the ground ahead, they see something huge, and bleeding.

teach.b: At first Rama thinks it's a demon that has eaten Sita, and he draws his bow. Then the bird speaks. It's Jatayu, and he's dying.
With what breath he has left, he tells them: Ravana took her. I fought him. He cut me down and flew south.
He tries to say more. Valmiki has him begin: Ravana, son of Vishravas, brother of Kubera, the lord of wealth. Then the words stop, and he dies.
He spends his last breath the way Sita spent her voice, on the message.
Holding the body, Rama tells Lakshmana that this bird lived long in the forest and has died for them, and deserves the same honor as their own father.
Remember, Rama wasn't there when Dasharatha's body was burned; he heard the news in the forest, from Bharata. Now Rama builds a pyre himself and performs the last rites for a vulture, as a son would.
He offers the water, and Valmiki says Jatayu goes to the highest worlds. Here's the teaching.

teach.h: ANTYESHTI: A SON'S RITES FOR A BIRD.
teach.b: Hindus call the last rites antyeshti, the final offering, and giving them is a sacred duty, dharma, usually carried by a son. Families still remember their dead with water offerings and rites called shraddha.
Rama shows who that duty can reach: not only blood, but anyone whose love made them family. And the first thing he does after learning who took Sita isn't revenge. It's a funeral.

how: Hindu funeral rites (antyeshti) are usually performed by a son or close relative, and families remember their dead with water offerings and shraddha rites; many teachers tell Rama's rites for Jatayu as a sign that loyalty can make someone family.

o: the vulture who guides Rama south to the sea's edge
a sage who performs the last rites for Rama's father
the vulture who spends his last breath on the message

games.q: the empty hut and the dying bird — tap the pairs.

s: Rama goes straight after Ravana when he learns the name
first he builds Jatayu a pyre and performs the last rites.
Jatayu dies before he can say where Ravana lives
he names Ravana's father and brother, and then his words stop.
in Hindu tradition, the last rites are usually a son's duty
and Rama, a prince, takes that duty on for a vulture who died for his family.

games.q: you're Rama. the vulture who fought for Sita has just died in front of you. what do you do?
o: leave at once to chase Ravana.
build a pyre and perform the last rites yourself.
ask Lakshmana to bury him while you go on.
games.why: Rama performs Jatayu's funeral himself, as a son for a father, before anything else.

practice: Many Hindus remember those who've died by offering a little water or lighting a lamp and saying their name. Bring to mind someone who helped you and is gone, or far away, or simply never thanked, and let their face come up.
If you pray, say their name once and offer your thanks, with a little water if you have it. If you don't, breathe in and remember one thing they did; breathe out and let the thanks be there.

wordCard.voice: Jatayu. His last breath goes to the message, and Rama gives him antyeshti, a son's last rites.

orig.note: Sanskrit gṛdhrarāja: king of vultures, a title Valmiki gives Jatayu.

carryVoice: Your line: the last rites honor love, not only blood. Tomorrow, the forest gets stranger still. See you tomorrow.
